title: Mistakes to avoid when you start AI training in Nepal
summary:
The costliest mistake in AI training in Nepal is paying for the wrong kind. Learning to use ChatGPT at work, learning to build AI apps, and doing paid "AI training" tasks are three different things, and each needs a different first step.

The other mistakes come after you pick. Most of them cost months, not money. Here they are, with what to do instead.

What does "AI training" mean in Nepal?

When you search for AI training in Nepal, most news results are about short workshops. They teach office staff, teachers and students to use AI tools well. That is useful, but it will not prepare you for an AI engineering job.

AI engineering is different. You write Python that calls a model, feeds it your own documents, tests its answers and runs it online for real users.

There is also a third meaning. Remote job boards post "AI training" work, where you rate AI answers, write code to grade them, or check Nepali text. That is a job, not a course.

Decide which one you want before you pay anyone. We wrote earlier about why AI and data science skills are in demand in Nepal. The rest of this article is about the second meaning: learning to build.

Do you need Python before you learn AI?

Yes. Skipping Python to jump straight to prompts is the mistake we would warn you about first. Every AI engineering tool you will use, from scikit-learn to LangChain, expects you to read and write Python.

Even the free Hugging Face LLM course says it "requires a good knowledge of Python". Without it, you copy code you cannot fix.

Classic machine learning matters too. Some problems, like sorting short texts into a few groups, are solved faster and cheaper by a simple model than by an LLM. Learn when that is true before you reach for the biggest tool.

Do you need a gaming laptop or a GPU for AI?

No. Do not buy new hardware to start. A normal laptop with 8GB of RAM is enough for the first months.

For heavy steps, use Google Colab. It is free, though its free GPU access is "heavily restricted" and a notebook can run for at most 12 hours. That is enough for learning.

To run a model on your own machine, install Ollama and type ollama run gemma4. On a laptop with 8GB, pick a small model. It will be slow, but once it is downloaded it runs without internet, which helps on days when the connection drops.

Should you pay for ChatGPT or Claude API credit to start?

Not yet. Google AI Studio has a free tier for the Gemini API, and Groq has a free plan too. You can learn prompts, structured outputs and streaming without a bank dollar card.

There is one catch. Google says content sent on the free tier is used to improve its products. So never paste company data, client files or anyone's personal details into a free-tier app.

Should you start with LangChain or agents?

Start without them. Call the model directly first, in a few lines of Python. Then you see exactly what goes in and what comes out.

Anthropic's guide on building effective agents gives the same advice. It says frameworks "often create extra layers of abstraction that can obscure the underlying prompts". It also recommends the simplest solution that works, and adding agents only when you need them.

Once you can build a small agent loop by hand, a framework saves you time. Before that, it hides your bugs.

Is a working demo enough?

No. A chatbot that answers your five test questions well can still fail on the sixth. Learn to measure answers against a fixed set of questions, and track what each request costs.

Learn safety early too. Prompt injection, where text tricks the model into ignoring your instructions, is first on the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications. Any app that reads emails, web pages or uploaded files is open to it.

How long is AI engineering training at Saarathi?

The AI Engineering and Machine Learning course at Saarathi Academy in Old Baneshwor, Kathmandu, runs for 12 weeks, in the order this article argues for.

Weeks 1 to 5 cover Python from zero, machine learning, NLP and deep learning before any LLM work. Week 4 includes a text classifier with a Nepali run, and a session on when a simple model beats an LLM. Class runs on free tiers, so you do not have to pay for API credit. In Week 9 you build the agent loop by hand before using LangChain. Week 10 covers evaluation and prompt injection.

The course is fast. Plan for 2 to 3 hours of practice every day on top of class. A laptop with 16GB of RAM is recommended, and 8GB works with small local models and free Colab. Each batch has up to 10 students in the classroom, and mentors still do the job they teach.

What to try tonight

Install Ollama, run ollama run gemma4, and ask it to explain one Python error you got this week. Then open Google AI Studio, make a free key, and call Gemini from a Python file. If that second step feels hard, spend a few weeks on Python basics first. Now you know where you stand.

The week-by-week plan is on our course page, and the full syllabus is public before you pay anything.

title: eBay Best Offer Accepted Price API: Get What Buyers Actually Paid (2026)
summary:
An eBay Best Offer accepted price API answers a question eBay itself won't: what did the buyer actually pay?

When a listing sells through an accepted Best Offer, eBay's sold page shows the original asking price, struck through. The negotiated price stays hidden. If you build comps, price inventory or run a valuation tool, those asking prices quietly push every number you calculate upward.

Here is a real example from last week. A PSA 10 Charizard VMAX 074/073 (Champion's Path) sold on October 25, 2026:

What eBay shows What the buyer paid
$349.00 (asking price) $307.00 (accepted offer)

That's $42, or 12%, off the price you'd have recorded. In the same search, 11 of 60 recent sales closed on a Best Offer. Average those in at the asking price and your "market value" is fiction.

This post shows how to get the real number with one request.

The short version 

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $COMPSNIPER_API_KEY" \
  "https://api.compsniper.com/v1/scrape?keyword=psa+10+charizard+vmax+074&count=100&bestOfferPrice=true"

Add bestOfferPrice=true to a sold search and every sale that closed on an accepted offer gains two fields:

{
  "title": "2020 Pokemon SWSH FA Charizard Vmax 074/073 Champion's Path Secret PSA 10",
  "bestOfferAccepted": true,
  "soldPrice": "349.00",
  "acceptedOfferPrice": "307.00",
  "acceptedOfferPriceStatus": "found",
  "endedAt": "2026-10-25"
}
  • soldPrice is untouched: it's still the listed price, so you can see the discount.
  • acceptedOfferPrice is what the buyer paid.
  • acceptedOfferPriceStatus tells you where that price stands: found, pending (still being looked up, check back shortly) or not_available.

No eBay developer account, no seller access to the transaction, no scraping on your side. The free plan includes 100 requests a month, and the accepted price costs nothing extra.

Why the official eBay APIs don't help here

If you've tried to solve this with eBay's own tools, you've hit these walls:

  • Trading API GetBestOffers only returns offers on your own listings. Useless for market comps.
  • Browse API returns active listings only. No sold prices at all.
  • Finding API findCompletedItems was decommissioned in February 2025.
  • Marketplace Insights API is a limited release for approved partners, and it isn't taking most new developers.

So the accepted price on other sellers' sales is simply not available from eBay to a regular developer. That's the gap this fills.

Python: comps with the real accepted prices 

import os
import statistics
import requests

def sold_comps(keyword, count=100):
    r = requests.get(
        "https://api.compsniper.com/v1/scrape",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['COMPSNIPER_API_KEY']}"},
        params={"keyword": keyword, "count": count, "bestOfferPrice": "true"},
        timeout=90,
    )
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()["items"]

def real_price(item):
    """Use the accepted offer when we have it, otherwise the sold price."""
    if item.get("bestOfferAccepted") and item.get("acceptedOfferPriceStatus") == "found":
        return float(item["acceptedOfferPrice"])
    return float(item["soldPrice"])

items = sold_comps("psa 10 charizard vmax 074")
asking = [float(i["soldPrice"]) for i in items]
paid = [real_price(i) for i in items]

print(f"median from eBay's displayed prices: ${statistics.median(asking):,.2f}")
print(f"median from what buyers paid:        ${statistics.median(paid):,.2f}")

for i in items:
    if i.get("acceptedOfferPriceStatus") == "found":
        print(f"{i['endedAt']}  asked ${i['soldPrice']}  paid ${i['acceptedOfferPrice']}  {i['title'][:60]}")

Prefer a package? pip install compsniper wraps the same calls with retries built in.

JavaScript (Node 18+, no dependencies) 

const params = new URLSearchParams({
  keyword: "psa 10 charizard vmax 074",
  count: "100",
  bestOfferPrice: "true",
});

const res = await fetch(`https://api.compsniper.com/v1/scrape?${params}`, {
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.COMPSNIPER_API_KEY}` },
});
if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`API error ${res.status}`);

const { items } = await res.json();
const realPrice = (i) =>
  i.bestOfferAccepted && i.acceptedOfferPriceStatus === "found"
    ? Number(i.acceptedOfferPrice)
    : Number(i.soldPrice);

for (const i of items.filter((x) => x.bestOfferAccepted)) {
  console.log(i.endedAt, "asked", i.soldPrice, "paid", i.acceptedOfferPrice ?? "(pending)", i.title);
}

What to do with pending

Accepted prices aren't always ready the moment a sale appears. A row marked pending is still being looked up. Two simple strategies:

  1. For a live price check, use the accepted price where it's found and fall back to the sold price elsewhere (the real_price helper above).
  2. For a database, store the item ID and re-check later. GET /v1/best-offer-prices?itemIds=... returns the latest status for up to 100 sales at once, so you can fill in the gaps on a schedule.

One more detail: accepted prices are returned for sales in US dollars on ebay.com. On other eBay sites, accepted-offer rows come back as not_available.

Where this matters most

  • Graded cards and collectibles: offers are everywhere, and a 10 to 15% gap on a $300 card is the difference between profit and loss.
  • Resale pricing tools: your users trust your "sold for" number. Asking prices make it wrong in the direction that hurts them.
  • Inventory valuation: one inflated comp per category compounds across thousands of SKUs.
  • Arbitrage bots: buying at the "market price" when the market really clears 12% lower is how bots lose money.

Try it

  1. Create a free account at compsniper.com and copy your API key.
  2. Run the curl above with your own search.
  3. Compare the two medians.

Full reference: Accepted Best Offer prices docs. Runnable examples: ebay-best-offer-price-api on GitHub.

Over to you: when you price items from eBay sold listings today, are you counting Best Offer sales at the asking price, or throwing them out entirely?

title: Pulling every tweet for a keyword into SQLite (and what each run actually costs)
summary:
I wanted a small local archive of posts about DuckDB: something I can query with plain SQL, re-run whenever I like, and not worry about duplicates. Here's the script I ended up with, the bill for each run, and the one mistake that made my second run cost as much as the first.

Disclosure: I work on TwitterAPI.io, the API used below. Written with AI assistance; the code and every number come from my own runs.

The query 

"duckdb" lang:en min_faves:20 -filter:replies

English posts that mention DuckDB, have at least 20 likes, and aren't replies. The min_faves filter keeps the archive to posts people actually engaged with, and it also keeps the bill down, because you pay per tweet returned.

The script

One file, standard library only. It pages through advanced_search (20 tweets per page), writes each tweet into SQLite keyed by its ID, and adds up the credits as it goes.

"""Collect every tweet for a search query into SQLite, page by page, and report the cost.

usage: TWITTERAPI_KEY=... python3 collect.py "" [max_pages]
Re-running is safe: tweets are keyed by id, so pages you already have are not duplicated.
"""
import json, os, sqlite3, sys, time, urllib.parse, urllib.request

API = "https://api.twitterapi.io/twitter/tweet/advanced_search"
KEY = os.environ["TWITTERAPI_KEY"]
query = sys.argv[1]
max_pages = int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 10

db = sqlite3.connect("tweets.db")
db.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS tweets (
    id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, query TEXT, created_at TEXT, author TEXT,
    text TEXT, likes INT, retweets INT, replies INT, raw TEXT)""")

def get_page(cursor):
    params = {"query": query, "queryType": "Latest", "cursor": cursor}
    req = urllib.request.Request(f"{API}?{urllib.parse.urlencode(params)}", headers={"X-API-Key": KEY})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=30) as r:
        return json.load(r)

cursor, calls, fetched, new, credits = "", 0, 0, 0, 0
started = time.time()
while calls < max_pages:
    page = get_page(cursor)
    calls += 1
    tweets = page.get("tweets") or []
    fetched += len(tweets)
    credits += max(len(tweets) * 15, 15)  # billed per request: 15 credits per tweet, 15 minimum
    page_new = 0
    for t in tweets:
        cur = db.execute("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO tweets VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?)", (
            t["id"], query, t.get("createdAt"), (t.get("author") or {}).get("userName"),
            t.get("text"), t.get("likeCount"), t.get("retweetCount"), t.get("replyCount"), json.dumps(t)))
        new += cur.rowcount; page_new += cur.rowcount
    db.commit()
    # "Latest" returns newest first: once a whole page is already stored, everything older is too.
    if tweets and page_new == 0:
        break
    if not page.get("has_next_page") or not tweets:
        break
    cursor = page.get("next_cursor") or ""

total = db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tweets WHERE query=?", (query,)).fetchone()[0]
cost = credits / 100_000  # 100,000 credits = $1
print(json.dumps({"query": query, "calls": calls, "tweets_returned": fetched, "new_rows": new,
                  "rows_in_db_for_query": total, "credits": credits, "cost_usd": round(cost, 5),
                  "seconds": round(time.time() - started, 1)}))

Run it:

export TWITTERAPI_KEY=...        # from your dashboard
python3 collect.py '"duckdb" lang:en min_faves:20 -filter:replies' 15

What it cost

The billing rule is simple: 15 credits per tweet returned, with a 15-credit minimum per request, and 100,000 credits = $1. A full page of 20 tweets is 300 credits, or $0.003. A request that returns nothing still costs 15 credits.

Run Requests Tweets returned New rows Credits Cost
1st run (empty database) 15 300 300 4,500 $0.045
2nd run, first version of the script 15 300 0 4,500 $0.045
2nd run, with the "stop on a known page" check 1 20 0 300 $0.003

The first run took about 45 seconds for 15 pages.

For scale: reading the same 300 posts through the official X API's pay-per-use tier at $0.005 per post read would be $1.50, about 33 times more per read.

The mistake: re-runs that pay for data you already have

My first version had no stop condition other than has_next_page. INSERT OR IGNORE meant no duplicate rows, so the database looked fine. But the second run walked the same 15 pages and paid for all 300 tweets again, while saving zero new ones.

The fix is the page_new == 0 check. With queryType=Latest the newest posts come first. So when the scheduled re-run reaches a page where every tweet is already stored, everything after it is already stored too, and it can stop. A daily re-run then costs about one page per 20 new posts, plus one page to confirm there is nothing newer.

Two caveats. First, this assumes the previous run finished: if a first backfill dies halfway, the next run sees the newest page as "known" and stops before reaching the gap. For long backfills, saving next_cursor after each page and resuming from it avoids this. Second, with a min_faves filter, posts that cross the threshold later show up deeper in the results; the stop check skips them, so run a full re-crawl now and then if you need them.

Querying it 

-- most-liked posts in the archive
SELECT likes, substr(text, 1, 80) FROM tweets ORDER BY likes DESC LIMIT 5;

-- posts per day
SELECT substr(created_at, 5, 6) AS day, COUNT(*) FROM tweets GROUP BY day ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC;

The raw column keeps the full JSON of each tweet, so you can add columns later without fetching again.

Notes if you try it

  • Rate limits: paid accounts get 20 requests per second. Free accounts are limited to 1 request every 5 seconds until credits are purchased, so add time.sleep(5) in the loop if you're on free credits.
  • Free credits: new accounts get up to $1 of free credits (bot check, one per person). That's enough for this whole exercise many times over.
  • Narrow queries save money: min_faves, lang: and -filter:replies cut the number of tweets returned, and returned tweets are what you pay for.

Pricing details are on the pricing page.

usage: TWITTERAPI_KEY=... python3 collect.py "" [max_pages]
Re-running is safe: tweets are keyed by id, so pages you already have are not duplicated.
"""
import json, os, sqlite3, sys, time, urllib.parse, urllib.request

API = "https://api.twitterapi.io/twitter/tweet/advanced_search"
KEY = os.environ["TWITTERAPI_KEY"]
query = sys.argv[1]
max_pages = int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 10

db = sqlite3.connect("tweets.db")
db.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS tweets (
    id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, query TEXT, created_at TEXT, author TEXT,
    text TEXT, likes INT, retweets INT, replies INT, raw TEXT)""")

def get_page(cursor):
    params = {"query": query, "queryType": "Latest", "cursor": cursor}
    req = urllib.request.Request(f"{API}?{urllib.parse.urlencode(params)}", headers={"X-API-Key": KEY})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=30) as r:
        return json.load(r)

cursor, calls, fetched, new, credits = "", 0, 0, 0, 0
started = time.time()
while calls < max_pages:
    page = get_page(cursor)
    calls += 1
    tweets = page.get("tweets") or []
    fetched += len(tweets)
    credits += max(len(tweets) * 15, 15)  # billed per request: 15 credits per tweet, 15 minimum
    page_new = 0
    for t in tweets:
        cur = db.execute("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO tweets VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?)", (
            t["id"], query, t.get("createdAt"), (t.get("author") or {}).get("userName"),
            t.get("text"), t.get("likeCount"), t.get("retweetCount"), t.get("replyCount"), json.dumps(t)))
        new += cur.rowcount; page_new += cur.rowcount
    db.commit()
    # "Latest" returns newest first: once a whole page is already stored, everything older is too.
    if tweets and page_new == 0:
        break
    if not page.get("has_next_page") or not tweets:
        break
    cursor = page.get("next_cursor") or ""

total = db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tweets WHERE query=?", (query,)).fetchone()[0]
cost = credits / 100_000  # 100,000 credits = $1
print(json.dumps({"query": query, "calls": calls, "tweets_returned": fetched, "new_rows": new,
                  "rows_in_db_for_query": total, "credits": credits, "cost_usd": round(cost, 5),
                  "seconds": round(time.time() - started, 1)}))

Run it:

export TWITTERAPI_KEY=...        # from your dashboard
python3 collect.py '"duckdb" lang:en min_faves:20 -filter:replies' 15

What it cost

The billing rule is simple: 15 credits per tweet returned, with a 15-credit minimum per request, and 100,000 credits = $1. A full page of 20 tweets is 300 credits, or $0.003. A request that returns nothing still costs 15 credits.

Run Requests Tweets returned New rows Credits Cost
1st run (empty database) 15 300 300 4,500 $0.045
2nd run, first version of the script 15 300 0 4,500 $0.045
2nd run, with the "stop on a known page" check 1 20 0 300 $0.003

The first run took about 45 seconds for 15 pages.

For scale: reading the same 300 posts through the official X API's pay-per-use tier at $0.005 per post read would be $1.50, about 33 times more per read.

The mistake: re-runs that pay for data you already have

My first version had no stop condition other than has_next_page. INSERT OR IGNORE meant no duplicate rows, so the database looked fine. But the second run walked the same 15 pages and paid for all 300 tweets again, while saving zero new ones.

The fix is the page_new == 0 check. With queryType=Latest the newest posts come first. So when the scheduled re-run reaches a page where every tweet is already stored, everything after it is already stored too, and it can stop. A daily re-run then costs about one page per 20 new posts, plus one page to confirm there is nothing newer.

Two caveats. First, this assumes the previous run finished: if a first backfill dies halfway, the next run sees the newest page as "known" and stops before reaching the gap. For long backfills, saving next_cursor after each page and resuming from it avoids this. Second, with a min_faves filter, posts that cross the threshold later show up deeper in the results; the stop check skips them, so run a full re-crawl now and then if you need them.

Querying it 

-- most-liked posts in the archive
SELECT likes, substr(text, 1, 80) FROM tweets ORDER BY likes DESC LIMIT 5;

-- posts per day
SELECT substr(created_at, 5, 6) AS day, COUNT(*) FROM tweets GROUP BY day ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC;

The raw column keeps the full JSON of each tweet, so you can add columns later without fetching again.

Notes if you try it

  • Rate limits: paid accounts get 20 requests per second. Free accounts are limited to 1 request every 5 seconds until credits are purchased, so add time.sleep(5) in the loop if you're on free credits.
  • Free credits: new accounts get up to $1 of free credits (bot check, one per person). That's enough for this whole exercise many times over.
  • Narrow queries save money: min_faves, lang: and -filter:replies cut the number of tweets returned, and returned tweets are what you pay for.

Pricing details are on the pricing page.

title: Your Code Has Bugs You Haven't Met Yet: A Friendly Deep Dive into SAST with SonarQube
summary:
"An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure."
— Benjamin Franklin

The bug that waited six months

Let me tell you about a Friday night that went sideways.

A team I know shipped a tiny feature: a search box on an internal admin dashboard. Two lines of code built a SQL query by gluing the user's input straight into a string. It passed code review. It passed QA. It worked perfectly for six months.

Then someone typed ' OR '1'='1 into that box. Every customer record came back in one page.

Here's the painful part: nobody was careless. The reviewer was looking at business logic, not string concatenation. QA was testing whether search worked, not whether it could be abused. The bug wasn't hidden. It was sitting in plain sight, in a pull request, waiting.

A tool that reads code for exactly this kind of mistake would have flagged it in seconds, before the merge button was ever clicked.

That tool category has a name: SAST. And one of the most popular ways to do it is SonarQube.

If the pattern feels familiar, it should. Injection is still a headline category: it sits at #5 in the OWASP Top 10:2025 (it was #3 in 2021). It dropped because the industry got better at it, not because it went away.

The post at a glance

  • Reading time: about 14 minutes
  • Hands-on time: about 10 minutes, with Docker
  • You will learn: what SAST is, how taint analysis works, how SonarQube is built, how to gate pull requests, and how to keep a team from muting the tool
  • You need: Docker, a project with some code, and a coffee

Here's the road map:

  • What SAST actually is (and what it isn't)
  • How a machine can "read" your code and spot a vulnerability
  • What SonarQube does, and how its pieces fit together
  • Running it locally with Docker in about ten minutes
  • Wiring it into CI so bad code can't sneak into main
  • The honest stuff: false positives, noisy dashboards, and how to get your team to actually care

Grab a coffee. Let's go.

So what is SAST, really?

SAST (Static Application Security Testing) reads your source code without running it, and looks for patterns that lead to security holes.

Think of it like a spell-checker, but for danger. A spell-checker doesn't need you to say the sentence out loud to know "recieve" is wrong. SAST doesn't need your app to run to know that user input is flowing straight into a SQL query.

The word that matters most is static. The code is just text on disk. No server, no database, no test data. That's what makes SAST so useful: it can run the moment you write a line, long before anything is deployed.

Where SAST fits among its cousins

You'll hear a pile of acronyms in AppSec conversations. Here's the cheat sheet:

Approach What it looks at When it runs Great at catching Blind spots
SAST (static) Your source code While coding, on every PR Injection, hardcoded secrets, unsafe APIs, crypto misuse Runtime config, server setup, business logic
DAST (dynamic) Your running app, from outside Against staging or test environments Misconfigured headers, auth issues, real exploitable endpoints Can't point to the exact line of code
SCA (composition) Your dependencies (npm, Maven, pip) On every build Known CVEs in third-party libraries Bugs in your code
IAST (interactive) The app from inside, while tests run During QA and integration tests Confirmed, real-path vulnerabilities Only sees code paths your tests exercise

None of these replaces the others. But if you can only start with one, SAST gives you the best bang for the buck. It's cheap, fast, and it talks to developers in their own language: file name, line number, here's why, here's the fix.

The "shift left" argument

You've probably heard "shift left." It just means: find problems earlier in the timeline, where they're cheaper to fix.

A vulnerability caught in your editor costs you thirty seconds. The same vulnerability caught in a penetration test costs a ticket, a context switch, a re-review and a redeploy. Caught in production by an attacker? That's an incident report, a lawyer, and possibly a news headline.

The shape is the point: effort multiplies at every stage. The numbers are an illustrative model, not measured data.

SAST is the most "left" security check you can run. It lives right next to your code.

How does a tool "read" code?

A SAST engine turns your code into a structured model, then asks questions about how data moves through it. It's less magic than it sounds. Let's peel it open, one layer at a time.

Step 1: From text to a tree

To you, code is text. To a SAST tool, text is useless until it's parsed into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST): a tree where every node is a meaningful piece, like a function call, a variable, or a string.

Take this tiny snippet, shown in Python and Node.js:

name = request.args.get("name")
sql = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'"
cursor.execute(sql)

const name = req.query.name;
const sql = `SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '${name}'`;
db.query(sql);

The tool no longer sees characters. It sees: a variable name assigned from request.args.get (or req.query), a string built by interpolation, and a call to execute (or query). Now it can reason.

Step 2: Simple rules (pattern matching)

The easiest checks just look at the tree's shape. "Is someone calling MD5 for password hashing?" "Is there a hardcoded string that looks like an AWS key?" "Is this catch block empty?"

These are fast and precise, but they only see one spot at a time.

Step 3: Following the data (taint analysis)

This is where SAST gets clever. Taint analysis tracks untrusted data as it travels through your program. It uses three ideas:

  • Source: where untrusted data enters. Think HTTP parameters, headers, file uploads, or message queues.
  • Sink: a dangerous place for that data to land. Think SQL queries, shell commands, file paths, or HTML output.
  • Sanitizer: something that makes the data safe on the way. Think parameterized queries, escaping, or strict validation.

The rule is simple: if tainted data reaches a sink without passing through a sanitizer, raise the alarm.

If the data passes a sanitizer, nothing is reported; if it reaches the sink untouched, you get a vulnerability.

In our snippet, request.args.get("name") (or req.query.name) is the source, cursor.execute(sql) (or db.query(sql)) is the sink, and nothing cleans the data in between. That's SQL injection, flagged before the code ever runs. And the real power is that the source and sink can live in different files, three function calls apart. A human reviewer looking at one diff would never connect them. The engine does.

The fix the tool will nudge you toward 

name = request.args.get("name")
sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?"
cursor.execute(sql, (name,))
rows = cursor.fetchall()

const name = req.query.name;
const sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = $1";
const { rows } = await db.query(sql, [name]);

The parameterized query acts as the sanitizer. The data can still be anything, but it can no longer change the shape of the SQL.

The placeholder depends on your driver: ? for sqlite3 and mysql2, %s for psycopg2, $1 for node-postgres. The idea is identical: the value travels separately from the query text.

A quick reality check

Static analysis has a famous trade-off. Being exhaustive means more false positives (alarms that aren't real). Being conservative means more false negatives (real bugs it misses). Every tool picks a spot on that dial. We'll come back to how to live with this later.

"Debugging is twice as hard as writing the code in the first place."
— Brian Kernighan, The Elements of Programming Style

Meet SonarQube

SonarQube is a code quality and security platform from SonarSource that runs SAST (and much more) on every branch and pull request, and turns the results into a simple pass/fail signal. It's been around since 2007, and it's probably the tool your company's platform team has already heard of.

What makes it different from a pure security scanner is its scope. SonarQube cares about the whole health of your code: security vulnerabilities, yes, but also reliability bugs, maintainability problems, duplication and test coverage. Security people love it for the first part. Developers tend to love it for the rest.

The family, untangled

SonarSource renamed things in 2024–2025, so blog posts online can be confusing. Here's today's lineup:

Product What it is Who it's for
SonarQube for IDE (formerly SonarLint) A free plugin for VS Code, IntelliJ, Visual Studio and Eclipse Every developer, catching issues as they type
SonarQube Community Build (formerly Community Edition) Free, open-source, self-hosted; released on a regular cadence Learning, small teams, single-branch analysis
SonarQube Server (Developer, Enterprise, Data Center editions) Commercial, self-hosted; branch and PR analysis, deeper taint analysis Teams who need PR decoration and full security coverage
SonarQube Cloud (formerly SonarCloud) The SaaS version, hosted by Sonar Teams who don't want to run a server; has a free tier

Two things worth knowing before you choose:

  • Server versions now use calendar numbering, like 2025.1. Some releases are marked LTA (Long-Term Active), which is what you want for a stable production install.
  • The free Community Build analyzes one branch and doesn't decorate pull requests. The heavier security analysis, including cross-file taint tracking, lives in the commercial editions and SonarQube Cloud. For learning and for this tutorial, Community Build is perfect.

The four ideas you need to know

Once you understand these, the whole SonarQube UI makes sense:

  1. Rules. A single check, like "SQL queries should not be built from user input." SonarQube ships with thousands of them across 30+ languages.
  2. Quality Profiles. A named set of rules per language. The default is called "Sonar way", and it's a sensible starting point. You can copy it and tune it.
  3. Quality Gates. The pass/fail verdict. A gate is a set of conditions, like "no new vulnerabilities" and "coverage on new code is at least 80%." If any condition fails, the gate fails, and your pipeline can stop the merge.
  4. New Code. SonarQube's secret weapon. Instead of shouting about ten years of legacy debt, it focuses on code you changed recently. More on this in a moment.

How the pieces talk to each other

The architecture is simpler than it looks. The scanner runs where your code is (your laptop or a CI runner). It does the analysis and uploads a report. The server processes that report, stores results in a database, and shows them in the web UI.

The important bit: your source code never has to leave your CI runner. Only the analysis report travels to the server.

Hands-on: your first scan in about ten minutes

You need Docker and a project with some code in it. That's it. We'll run the free Community Build locally and scan a deliberately vulnerable snippet.

1. Start the server 

docker run -d --name sonarqube \
  -p 9000:9000 \
  sonarqube:community

Give it a minute or two to boot (it starts an Elasticsearch instance inside, so it's not instant). Then open http://localhost:9000 and log in with admin / admin. It'll ask you to change the password right away.

Heads up: this quick-start uses an embedded H2 database. It's fine for a demo, but never use it in production. For a real install, point SonarQube at PostgreSQL with a docker-compose.yml. On Linux you may also need sysctl -w vm.max_map_count=524288 for Elasticsearch to start.

2. Create a project and a token

In the UI:

  1. Click Create Project → Local project.
  2. Give it a key, for example my-first-scan.
  3. For the baseline, choose Previous version as the definition of "new code."
  4. Choose Locally as the analysis method and generate a token. Copy it somewhere safe; you'll see it only once.

3. Add some deliberately bad code

Let's give the scanner something to find. Save this as app.py in an empty folder:

import sqlite3
import hashlib
from flask import Flask, request

app = Flask(__name__)
AWS_SECRET = "AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE"   # hardcoded credential

@app.route("/user")
def get_user():
    name = request.args.get("name")                # source
    conn = sqlite3.connect("app.db")
    query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'"
    return str(conn.execute(query).fetchall())     # sink

def hash_password(pw):
    return hashlib.md5(pw.encode()).hexdigest()   # weak hashing

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(debug=True)                            # debug in prod

Four problems, hiding in about twenty lines. Let's see how many get caught.

4. Run the scanner

The easiest way is the scanner's own Docker image, so you don't install anything:

docker run --rm \
  --network host \
  -e SONAR_HOST_URL="http://localhost:9000" \
  -e SONAR_TOKEN="" \
  -v "$(pwd):/usr/src" \
  sonarsource/sonar-scanner-cli \
  -Dsonar.projectKey=my-first-scan

On macOS or Windows, swap localhost for host.docker.internal and drop --network host.

Projects you'll scan again and again deserve a config file. Drop a sonar-project.properties at the root:

sonar.projectKey=my-first-scan
sonar.projectName=My First Scan
sonar.sources=.
sonar.exclusions=**/tests/**,**/node_modules/**
sonar.python.version=3.12

Python projects use the scanner CLI or the Docker image above, with the sonar-project.properties file you just wrote. There's no build plugin to add, so the same command works on your laptop and in CI.

JavaScript and TypeScript projects can skip Docker and run the npm scanner directly, with no install step:

npx @sonar/scan   -Dsonar.host.url=http://localhost:9000   -Dsonar.token=   -Dsonar.projectKey=my-first-scan

Without -Dsonar.projectKey, it takes the key from the name field in package.json.

5. Look at the dashboard

Refresh the project page. Expect the hardcoded secret, the weak MD5 hash and the Flask debug mode to show up, either as issues or as Security Hotspots depending on the rule and your version.

The SQL injection is the interesting one. It needs cross-function taint analysis, which lives in the commercial editions. On Community Build it may not be reported at all. That's not a bug in your test; it's the edition boundary, and it's a good reason to know what your tier can and can't see. The next section explains the hotspot idea.

Reading the report without panicking

Your first dashboard will probably show hundreds of issues. That's normal, and you don't have to fix them all. Let's decode what you're looking at.

Issue types, in human terms

SonarQube sorts findings by which quality of your software they hurt:

What you see What it means Example What to do
Vulnerability (Security) The tool is confident this is exploitable SQL built from request data, reaching execute() Fix it. Usually before merging.
Security Hotspot Security-sensitive code that needs a human to judge Using random(), a permissive CORS setting, a regex that could be slow Review it and mark it Safe or Fix
Bug (Reliability) Code that will likely misbehave Null dereference, unclosed resource, always-true condition Fix it; these become production incidents
Code Smell (Maintainability) Code that works but is hard to change 200-line function, duplicated blocks, deep nesting Fix when you touch that code

Each issue also carries a severity (Blocker, High, Medium, Low, Info) and a Clean Code attribute explaining why it matters. Click any issue and you'll get the exact line, a description of the risk, and usually a compliant code example. This is where developers actually learn something.

Not sure what to do with a finding? Follow the flow:

Every finding ends in one of three outcomes: fix it, justify it, or defer it on purpose.

Hotspots are not vulnerabilities

This trips up nearly everyone. A Vulnerability is SonarQube saying: "This is a problem." A Hotspot is SonarQube saying: "This could be a problem, and only you know the context."

Using a non-cryptographic random number is fine for shuffling a playlist. It's a disaster for generating a password reset token. The tool can't know which one you're doing, so it asks. Your job is to review hotspots, not ignore them.

The ratings

The dashboard grades Security, Reliability and Maintainability from A (best) to E. A single unresolved critical vulnerability can drag your Security rating to D or E. That's intentional: one real hole matters more than a thousand smells.

"Clean as You Code": the idea that saves your sanity

Imagine scanning a ten-year-old codebase for the first time. 4,000 issues. Your team will look at that number, sigh, and close the tab forever.

SonarQube's answer is a philosophy called Clean as You Code:

Don't try to fix the past. Just make sure every new change is clean.

It's the Boy Scout rule in a CI pipeline:

"Leave the campground cleaner than you found it."
— The Boy Scout rule, popularized in Clean Code by Robert C. Martin

The default Quality Gate, "Sonar way", only judges new code: the lines added or changed since your baseline. It checks roughly that new code has:

  • 0 new issues
  • 100% of new Security Hotspots reviewed
  • At least 80% test coverage
  • At most 3% duplication

The magic is that legacy code gets cleaner over time anyway, because every file you touch for a new feature gets held to the new standard. No "cleanup sprint" required. Old debt fades, new debt never arrives.

Putting it in your pipeline

A scan you run by hand is a scan you'll forget. The real value comes when every pull request is scanned automatically and the Quality Gate can block the merge.

Here's the flow we're building. A developer opens a PR, CI runs tests and the scanner, SonarQube judges the new code, and the result comes back as a status check on the PR.

The loop is the point: a red gate doesn't end the conversation, it just sends the change back for one more push.

GitHub Actions example

First, add two repository secrets under Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions:

  • SONAR_TOKEN: a token generated in SonarQube (use a project analysis token, not your admin token)
  • SONAR_HOST_URL: your server's URL, like https://sonar.yourcompany.com

Then create .github/workflows/sonarqube.yml:

Python:

name: SonarQube Analysis

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened]

jobs:
  sonarqube:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0   # full history = accurate "new code" and blame data

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: Run tests with coverage
        run: |
          pip install -r requirements.txt pytest pytest-cov
          pytest --cov=. --cov-report=xml

      - name: SonarQube Scan
        uses: SonarSource/sonarqube-scan-action@v5
        env:
          SONAR_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SONAR_TOKEN }}
          SONAR_HOST_URL: ${{ secrets.SONAR_HOST_URL }}
        with:
          args: >
            -Dsonar.python.coverage.reportPaths=coverage.xml
            -Dsonar.qualitygate.wait=true

JavaScript (Node.js):

name: SonarQube Analysis

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened]

jobs:
  sonarqube:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0   # full history = accurate "new code" and blame data

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22

      - name: Run tests with coverage
        run: |
          npm ci
          npx jest --coverage --coverageReporters=lcov

      - name: SonarQube Scan
        uses: SonarSource/sonarqube-scan-action@v5
        env:
          SONAR_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SONAR_TOKEN }}
          SONAR_HOST_URL: ${{ secrets.SONAR_HOST_URL }}
        with:
          args: >
            -Dsonar.javascript.lcov.reportPaths=coverage/lcov.info
            -Dsonar.qualitygate.wait=true

A few lines deserve a closer look:

  • fetch-depth: 0 is the most-forgotten line in every SonarQube setup. Without the full Git history, SonarQube can't tell which lines are new, and "Clean as You Code" quietly breaks.
  • sonar.qualitygate.wait=true makes the job wait for SonarQube's verdict and fail if the gate fails. That red X is what stops the merge.
  • Coverage is generated by your tests, not by SonarQube. SonarQube only reads the report. No report, no coverage number.
  • The Python property reads Cobertura XML, which pytest-cov writes as coverage.xml. The JavaScript property reads LCOV, which Jest writes to coverage/lcov.info.

The @v5 above is an example. Newer major versions of the action exist, so check the releases page, pin to a release you've verified, and update it on purpose, not by accident.

Making the gate actually block merges

The workflow failing isn't enough on its own. Go to Settings → Branches → Branch protection rules for main, enable Require status checks to pass, and select the SonarQube job. Now a failed Quality Gate physically blocks the merge button.

On SonarQube Server Developer Edition and above, or SonarQube Cloud, you also get PR decoration: a comment on the pull request summarizing new issues, with links straight to the problem lines. Developers see the feedback where they already are, which matters more than you'd think.

Using GitLab, Jenkins or Azure DevOps?

Same idea, different syntax. SonarQube has official integrations for GitLab CI, Azure Pipelines, Bitbucket Pipelines and Jenkins (via the SonarQube Scanner plugin plus a waitForQualityGate step). The three essentials stay identical: full Git history, a coverage report, and waiting for the gate.

The honest part: false positives, noise, and people

The hardest part of SAST is not installing the tool. It's getting a team to trust it. A scanner that cries wolf gets muted. Here's how to avoid that fate.

Dealing with false positives

You will see findings that aren't real problems. When that happens, resist the urge to silence everything. Instead:

  • Mark it in the UI, not in code. In SonarQube, set the issue to False Positive or Accepted and leave a short comment explaining why. Future you, and your auditor, will thank you.
  • Use // NOSONAR sparingly. It suppresses every issue on that line, silently, forever. It's the duct tape of static analysis. Some teams ban it outright in code review.
  • Tune the Quality Profile if one rule is consistently wrong for your codebase. Copy "Sonar way", deactivate that rule, and document the decision. Never edit the built-in profile directly.
  • Exclude what isn't yours. Generated code, vendored libraries, migrations and test fixtures inflate the noise. Use sonar.exclusions and sonar.test.exclusions.

Common mistakes I see over and over

  1. Shallow clones in CI. No full history means broken "new code" detection. (Yes, again. It's that common.)
  2. Scanning before tests. Coverage shows 0% and the gate fails for the wrong reason.
  3. Gating on overall code instead of new code. The gate fails on day one for legacy reasons, and the team learns to ignore red.
  4. One shared admin token in every pipeline. Use project-scoped analysis tokens and rotate them.
  5. Treating SonarQube as the whole security program. It doesn't scan your dependencies for known CVEs the way a dedicated SCA tool does (newer commercial editions add SCA as an option), and it never sees your runtime config. Pair it with SCA, secrets scanning and DAST.
  6. Running H2 in production. It's for demos only. Use PostgreSQL.

Rolling it out to a real team

The rollout plan that works tends to look like this:

Four steps, and the gate only turns on in week 3, after people have had time to get curious.

  1. Week 1, observe. Turn on scanning in CI, but don't block anything. Let people look at the dashboard and get curious.
  2. Week 2, install the IDE plugin. Get every developer on SonarQube for IDE in connected mode, so their editor uses the same rules as the server. Catching issues while typing is far less annoying than catching them in CI.
  3. Week 3, enable the gate on new code only. Use "Sonar way" as-is. Announce it, explain Clean as You Code, and answer questions.
  4. Ongoing, review together. Spend fifteen minutes in a retro now and then looking at hotspots and false positives. Tune the profile as a team.

The pattern underneath: make the tool a teammate, not a cop. Developers adopt tools that make them better at their job. They route around tools that only make them slower.

Wrapping up

Remember that search box from the start? With SonarQube in the pipeline, that PR would have come back red in a few minutes, with the exact line and a fix example attached. No incident, no Friday night, no awkward meeting.

That's the whole promise of SAST: catch the boring, predictable, expensive mistakes while they're still cheap. Not because developers are careless, but because humans are bad at spotting the same pattern for the thousandth time, and machines are great at it.

"We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act, but a habit."
— Will Durant, summarizing Aristotle

Your quick-start checklist

  • [ ] Run SonarQube Community Build locally with Docker
  • [ ] Scan one real project and skim the dashboard
  • [ ] Install SonarQube for IDE in your editor
  • [ ] Add the scanner to CI with fetch-depth: 0 and a coverage report
  • [ ] Turn on sonar.qualitygate.wait=true
  • [ ] Protect main so a failed gate blocks the merge
  • [ ] Gate on new code only, with "Sonar way"
  • [ ] Review hotspots; mark false positives with a reason
  • [ ] Pair it with dependency scanning (SCA) and secrets scanning

Over to you

Start small. Scan one repo this week. You'll almost certainly find something that makes you go "huh, how long has that been there?"

event_model_payload.summary:
"An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure."
— Benjamin Franklin

The bug that waited six months

Let me tell you about a Friday night that went sideways.

A team I know shipped a tiny feature: a search box on an internal admin dashboard. Two lines of code built a SQL query by gluing the user's input straight into a string. It passed code review. It passed QA. It worked perfectly for six months.

Then someone typed ' OR '1'='1 into that box. Every customer record came back in one page.

Here's the painful part: nobody was careless. The reviewer was looking at business logic, not string concatenation. QA was testing whether search worked, not whether it could be abused. The bug wasn't hidden. It was sitting in plain sight, in a pull request, waiting.

A tool that reads code for exactly this kind of mistake would have flagged it in seconds, before the merge button was ever clicked.

That tool category has a name: SAST. And one of the most popular ways to do it is SonarQube.

If the pattern feels familiar, it should. Injection is still a headline category: it sits at #5 in the OWASP Top 10:2025 (it was #3 in 2021). It dropped because the industry got better at it, not because it went away.

The post at a glance

  • Reading time: about 14 minutes
  • Hands-on time: about 10 minutes, with Docker
  • You will learn: what SAST is, how taint analysis works, how SonarQube is built, how to gate pull requests, and how to keep a team from muting the tool
  • You need: Docker, a project with some code, and a coffee

Here's the road map:

  • What SAST actually is (and what it isn't)
  • How a machine can "read" your code and spot a vulnerability
  • What SonarQube does, and how its pieces fit together
  • Running it locally with Docker in about ten minutes
  • Wiring it into CI so bad code can't sneak into main
  • The honest stuff: false positives, noisy dashboards, and how to get your team to actually care

Grab a coffee. Let's go.

So what is SAST, really?

SAST (Static Application Security Testing) reads your source code without running it, and looks for patterns that lead to security holes.

Think of it like a spell-checker, but for danger. A spell-checker doesn't need you to say the sentence out loud to know "recieve" is wrong. SAST doesn't need your app to run to know that user input is flowing straight into a SQL query.

The word that matters most is static. The code is just text on disk. No server, no database, no test data. That's what makes SAST so useful: it can run the moment you write a line, long before anything is deployed.

Where SAST fits among its cousins

You'll hear a pile of acronyms in AppSec conversations. Here's the cheat sheet:

Approach What it looks at When it runs Great at catching Blind spots
SAST (static) Your source code While coding, on every PR Injection, hardcoded secrets, unsafe APIs, crypto misuse Runtime config, server setup, business logic
DAST (dynamic) Your running app, from outside Against staging or test environments Misconfigured headers, auth issues, real exploitable endpoints Can't point to the exact line of code
SCA (composition) Your dependencies (npm, Maven, pip) On every build Known CVEs in third-party libraries Bugs in your code
IAST (interactive) The app from inside, while tests run During QA and integration tests Confirmed, real-path vulnerabilities Only sees code paths your tests exercise

None of these replaces the others. But if you can only start with one, SAST gives you the best bang for the buck. It's cheap, fast, and it talks to developers in their own language: file name, line number, here's why, here's the fix.

The "shift left" argument

You've probably heard "shift left." It just means: find problems earlier in the timeline, where they're cheaper to fix.

A vulnerability caught in your editor costs you thirty seconds. The same vulnerability caught in a penetration test costs a ticket, a context switch, a re-review and a redeploy. Caught in production by an attacker? That's an incident report, a lawyer, and possibly a news headline.

The shape is the point: effort multiplies at every stage. The numbers are an illustrative model, not measured data.

SAST is the most "left" security check you can run. It lives right next to your code.

How does a tool "read" code?

A SAST engine turns your code into a structured model, then asks questions about how data moves through it. It's less magic than it sounds. Let's peel it open, one layer at a time.

Step 1: From text to a tree

To you, code is text. To a SAST tool, text is useless until it's parsed into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST): a tree where every node is a meaningful piece, like a function call, a variable, or a string.

Take this tiny snippet, shown in Python and Node.js:

name = request.args.get("name")
sql = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'"
cursor.execute(sql)

const name = req.query.name;
const sql = `SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '${name}'`;
db.query(sql);

The tool no longer sees characters. It sees: a variable name assigned from request.args.get (or req.query), a string built by interpolation, and a call to execute (or query). Now it can reason.

Step 2: Simple rules (pattern matching)

The easiest checks just look at the tree's shape. "Is someone calling MD5 for password hashing?" "Is there a hardcoded string that looks like an AWS key?" "Is this catch block empty?"

These are fast and precise, but they only see one spot at a time.

Step 3: Following the data (taint analysis)

This is where SAST gets clever. Taint analysis tracks untrusted data as it travels through your program. It uses three ideas:

  • Source: where untrusted data enters. Think HTTP parameters, headers, file uploads, or message queues.
  • Sink: a dangerous place for that data to land. Think SQL queries, shell commands, file paths, or HTML output.
  • Sanitizer: something that makes the data safe on the way. Think parameterized queries, escaping, or strict validation.

The rule is simple: if tainted data reaches a sink without passing through a sanitizer, raise the alarm.

If the data passes a sanitizer, nothing is reported; if it reaches the sink untouched, you get a vulnerability.

In our snippet, request.args.get("name") (or req.query.name) is the source, cursor.execute(sql) (or db.query(sql)) is the sink, and nothing cleans the data in between. That's SQL injection, flagged before the code ever runs. And the real power is that the source and sink can live in different files, three function calls apart. A human reviewer looking at one diff would never connect them. The engine does.

The fix the tool will nudge you toward 

name = request.args.get("name")
sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?"
cursor.execute(sql, (name,))
rows = cursor.fetchall()

const name = req.query.name;
const sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = $1";
const { rows } = await db.query(sql, [name]);

The parameterized query acts as the sanitizer. The data can still be anything, but it can no longer change the shape of the SQL.

The placeholder depends on your driver: ? for sqlite3 and mysql2, %s for psycopg2, $1 for node-postgres. The idea is identical: the value travels separately from the query text.

A quick reality check

Static analysis has a famous trade-off. Being exhaustive means more false positives (alarms that aren't real). Being conservative means more false negatives (real bugs it misses). Every tool picks a spot on that dial. We'll come back to how to live with this later.

"Debugging is twice as hard as writing the code in the first place."
— Brian Kernighan, The Elements of Programming Style

Meet SonarQube

SonarQube is a code quality and security platform from SonarSource that runs SAST (and much more) on every branch and pull request, and turns the results into a simple pass/fail signal. It's been around since 2007, and it's probably the tool your company's platform team has already heard of.

What makes it different from a pure security scanner is its scope. SonarQube cares about the whole health of your code: security vulnerabilities, yes, but also reliability bugs, maintainability problems, duplication and test coverage. Security people love it for the first part. Developers tend to love it for the rest.

The family, untangled

SonarSource renamed things in 2024–2025, so blog posts online can be confusing. Here's today's lineup:

Product What it is Who it's for
SonarQube for IDE (formerly SonarLint) A free plugin for VS Code, IntelliJ, Visual Studio and Eclipse Every developer, catching issues as they type
SonarQube Community Build (formerly Community Edition) Free, open-source, self-hosted; released on a regular cadence Learning, small teams, single-branch analysis
SonarQube Server (Developer, Enterprise, Data Center editions) Commercial, self-hosted; branch and PR analysis, deeper taint analysis Teams who need PR decoration and full security coverage
SonarQube Cloud (formerly SonarCloud) The SaaS version, hosted by Sonar Teams who don't want to run a server; has a free tier

Two things worth knowing before you choose:

  • Server versions now use calendar numbering, like 2025.1. Some releases are marked LTA (Long-Term Active), which is what you want for a stable production install.
  • The free Community Build analyzes one branch and doesn't decorate pull requests. The heavier security analysis, including cross-file taint tracking, lives in the commercial editions and SonarQube Cloud. For learning and for this tutorial, Community Build is perfect.

The four ideas you need to know

Once you understand these, the whole SonarQube UI makes sense:

  1. Rules. A single check, like "SQL queries should not be built from user input." SonarQube ships with thousands of them across 30+ languages.
  2. Quality Profiles. A named set of rules per language. The default is called "Sonar way", and it's a sensible starting point. You can copy it and tune it.
  3. Quality Gates. The pass/fail verdict. A gate is a set of conditions, like "no new vulnerabilities" and "coverage on new code is at least 80%." If any condition fails, the gate fails, and your pipeline can stop the merge.
  4. New Code. SonarQube's secret weapon. Instead of shouting about ten years of legacy debt, it focuses on code you changed recently. More on this in a moment.

How the pieces talk to each other

The architecture is simpler than it looks. The scanner runs where your code is (your laptop or a CI runner). It does the analysis and uploads a report. The server processes that report, stores results in a database, and shows them in the web UI.

The important bit: your source code never has to leave your CI runner. Only the analysis report travels to the server.

Hands-on: your first scan in about ten minutes

You need Docker and a project with some code in it. That's it. We'll run the free Community Build locally and scan a deliberately vulnerable snippet.

1. Start the server 

docker run -d --name sonarqube \
  -p 9000:9000 \
  sonarqube:community

Give it a minute or two to boot (it starts an Elasticsearch instance inside, so it's not instant). Then open http://localhost:9000 and log in with admin / admin. It'll ask you to change the password right away.

Heads up: this quick-start uses an embedded H2 database. It's fine for a demo, but never use it in production. For a real install, point SonarQube at PostgreSQL with a docker-compose.yml. On Linux you may also need sysctl -w vm.max_map_count=524288 for Elasticsearch to start.

2. Create a project and a token

In the UI:

  1. Click Create Project → Local project.
  2. Give it a key, for example my-first-scan.
  3. For the baseline, choose Previous version as the definition of "new code."
  4. Choose Locally as the analysis method and generate a token. Copy it somewhere safe; you'll see it only once.

3. Add some deliberately bad code

Let's give the scanner something to find. Save this as app.py in an empty folder:

import sqlite3
import hashlib
from flask import Flask, request

app = Flask(__name__)
AWS_SECRET = "AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE"   # hardcoded credential

@app.route("/user")
def get_user():
    name = request.args.get("name")                # source
    conn = sqlite3.connect("app.db")
    query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'"
    return str(conn.execute(query).fetchall())     # sink

def hash_password(pw):
    return hashlib.md5(pw.encode()).hexdigest()   # weak hashing

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(debug=True)                            # debug in prod

Four problems, hiding in about twenty lines. Let's see how many get caught.

4. Run the scanner

The easiest way is the scanner's own Docker image, so you don't install anything:

docker run --rm \
  --network host \
  -e SONAR_HOST_URL="http://localhost:9000" \
  -e SONAR_TOKEN="" \
  -v "$(pwd):/usr/src" \
  sonarsource/sonar-scanner-cli \
  -Dsonar.projectKey=my-first-scan

On macOS or Windows, swap localhost for host.docker.internal and drop --network host.

Projects you'll scan again and again deserve a config file. Drop a sonar-project.properties at the root:

sonar.projectKey=my-first-scan
sonar.projectName=My First Scan
sonar.sources=.
sonar.exclusions=**/tests/**,**/node_modules/**
sonar.python.version=3.12

Python projects use the scanner CLI or the Docker image above, with the sonar-project.properties file you just wrote. There's no build plugin to add, so the same command works on your laptop and in CI.

JavaScript and TypeScript projects can skip Docker and run the npm scanner directly, with no install step:

npx @sonar/scan   -Dsonar.host.url=http://localhost:9000   -Dsonar.token=   -Dsonar.projectKey=my-first-scan

Without -Dsonar.projectKey, it takes the key from the name field in package.json.

5. Look at the dashboard

Refresh the project page. Expect the hardcoded secret, the weak MD5 hash and the Flask debug mode to show up, either as issues or as Security Hotspots depending on the rule and your version.

The SQL injection is the interesting one. It needs cross-function taint analysis, which lives in the commercial editions. On Community Build it may not be reported at all. That's not a bug in your test; it's the edition boundary, and it's a good reason to know what your tier can and can't see. The next section explains the hotspot idea.

Reading the report without panicking

Your first dashboard will probably show hundreds of issues. That's normal, and you don't have to fix them all. Let's decode what you're looking at.

Issue types, in human terms

SonarQube sorts findings by which quality of your software they hurt:

What you see What it means Example What to do
Vulnerability (Security) The tool is confident this is exploitable SQL built from request data, reaching execute() Fix it. Usually before merging.
Security Hotspot Security-sensitive code that needs a human to judge Using random(), a permissive CORS setting, a regex that could be slow Review it and mark it Safe or Fix
Bug (Reliability) Code that will likely misbehave Null dereference, unclosed resource, always-true condition Fix it; these become production incidents
Code Smell (Maintainability) Code that works but is hard to change 200-line function, duplicated blocks, deep nesting Fix when you touch that code

Each issue also carries a severity (Blocker, High, Medium, Low, Info) and a Clean Code attribute explaining why it matters. Click any issue and you'll get the exact line, a description of the risk, and usually a compliant code example. This is where developers actually learn something.

Not sure what to do with a finding? Follow the flow:

Every finding ends in one of three outcomes: fix it, justify it, or defer it on purpose.

Hotspots are not vulnerabilities

This trips up nearly everyone. A Vulnerability is SonarQube saying: "This is a problem." A Hotspot is SonarQube saying: "This could be a problem, and only you know the context."

Using a non-cryptographic random number is fine for shuffling a playlist. It's a disaster for generating a password reset token. The tool can't know which one you're doing, so it asks. Your job is to review hotspots, not ignore them.

The ratings

The dashboard grades Security, Reliability and Maintainability from A (best) to E. A single unresolved critical vulnerability can drag your Security rating to D or E. That's intentional: one real hole matters more than a thousand smells.

"Clean as You Code": the idea that saves your sanity

Imagine scanning a ten-year-old codebase for the first time. 4,000 issues. Your team will look at that number, sigh, and close the tab forever.

SonarQube's answer is a philosophy called Clean as You Code:

Don't try to fix the past. Just make sure every new change is clean.

It's the Boy Scout rule in a CI pipeline:

"Leave the campground cleaner than you found it."
— The Boy Scout rule, popularized in Clean Code by Robert C. Martin

The default Quality Gate, "Sonar way", only judges new code: the lines added or changed since your baseline. It checks roughly that new code has:

  • 0 new issues
  • 100% of new Security Hotspots reviewed
  • At least 80% test coverage
  • At most 3% duplication

The magic is that legacy code gets cleaner over time anyway, because every file you touch for a new feature gets held to the new standard. No "cleanup sprint" required. Old debt fades, new debt never arrives.

Putting it in your pipeline

A scan you run by hand is a scan you'll forget. The real value comes when every pull request is scanned automatically and the Quality Gate can block the merge.

Here's the flow we're building. A developer opens a PR, CI runs tests and the scanner, SonarQube judges the new code, and the result comes back as a status check on the PR.

The loop is the point: a red gate doesn't end the conversation, it just sends the change back for one more push.

GitHub Actions example

First, add two repository secrets under Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions:

  • SONAR_TOKEN: a token generated in SonarQube (use a project analysis token, not your admin token)
  • SONAR_HOST_URL: your server's URL, like https://sonar.yourcompany.com

Then create .github/workflows/sonarqube.yml:

Python:

name: SonarQube Analysis

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened]

jobs:
  sonarqube:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0   # full history = accurate "new code" and blame data

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: Run tests with coverage
        run: |
          pip install -r requirements.txt pytest pytest-cov
          pytest --cov=. --cov-report=xml

      - name: SonarQube Scan
        uses: SonarSource/sonarqube-scan-action@v5
        env:
          SONAR_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SONAR_TOKEN }}
          SONAR_HOST_URL: ${{ secrets.SONAR_HOST_URL }}
        with:
          args: >
            -Dsonar.python.coverage.reportPaths=coverage.xml
            -Dsonar.qualitygate.wait=true

JavaScript (Node.js):

name: SonarQube Analysis

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened]

jobs:
  sonarqube:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0   # full history = accurate "new code" and blame data

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22

      - name: Run tests with coverage
        run: |
          npm ci
          npx jest --coverage --coverageReporters=lcov

      - name: SonarQube Scan
        uses: SonarSource/sonarqube-scan-action@v5
        env:
          SONAR_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SONAR_TOKEN }}
          SONAR_HOST_URL: ${{ secrets.SONAR_HOST_URL }}
        with:
          args: >
            -Dsonar.javascript.lcov.reportPaths=coverage/lcov.info
            -Dsonar.qualitygate.wait=true

A few lines deserve a closer look:

  • fetch-depth: 0 is the most-forgotten line in every SonarQube setup. Without the full Git history, SonarQube can't tell which lines are new, and "Clean as You Code" quietly breaks.
  • sonar.qualitygate.wait=true makes the job wait for SonarQube's verdict and fail if the gate fails. That red X is what stops the merge.
  • Coverage is generated by your tests, not by SonarQube. SonarQube only reads the report. No report, no coverage number.
  • The Python property reads Cobertura XML, which pytest-cov writes as coverage.xml. The JavaScript property reads LCOV, which Jest writes to coverage/lcov.info.

The @v5 above is an example. Newer major versions of the action exist, so check the releases page, pin to a release you've verified, and update it on purpose, not by accident.

Making the gate actually block merges

The workflow failing isn't enough on its own. Go to Settings → Branches → Branch protection rules for main, enable Require status checks to pass, and select the SonarQube job. Now a failed Quality Gate physically blocks the merge button.

On SonarQube Server Developer Edition and above, or SonarQube Cloud, you also get PR decoration: a comment on the pull request summarizing new issues, with links straight to the problem lines. Developers see the feedback where they already are, which matters more than you'd think.

Using GitLab, Jenkins or Azure DevOps?

Same idea, different syntax. SonarQube has official integrations for GitLab CI, Azure Pipelines, Bitbucket Pipelines and Jenkins (via the SonarQube Scanner plugin plus a waitForQualityGate step). The three essentials stay identical: full Git history, a coverage report, and waiting for the gate.

The honest part: false positives, noise, and people

The hardest part of SAST is not installing the tool. It's getting a team to trust it. A scanner that cries wolf gets muted. Here's how to avoid that fate.

Dealing with false positives

You will see findings that aren't real problems. When that happens, resist the urge to silence everything. Instead:

  • Mark it in the UI, not in code. In SonarQube, set the issue to False Positive or Accepted and leave a short comment explaining why. Future you, and your auditor, will thank you.
  • Use // NOSONAR sparingly. It suppresses every issue on that line, silently, forever. It's the duct tape of static analysis. Some teams ban it outright in code review.
  • Tune the Quality Profile if one rule is consistently wrong for your codebase. Copy "Sonar way", deactivate that rule, and document the decision. Never edit the built-in profile directly.
  • Exclude what isn't yours. Generated code, vendored libraries, migrations and test fixtures inflate the noise. Use sonar.exclusions and sonar.test.exclusions.

Common mistakes I see over and over

  1. Shallow clones in CI. No full history means broken "new code" detection. (Yes, again. It's that common.)
  2. Scanning before tests. Coverage shows 0% and the gate fails for the wrong reason.
  3. Gating on overall code instead of new code. The gate fails on day one for legacy reasons, and the team learns to ignore red.
  4. One shared admin token in every pipeline. Use project-scoped analysis tokens and rotate them.
  5. Treating SonarQube as the whole security program. It doesn't scan your dependencies for known CVEs the way a dedicated SCA tool does (newer commercial editions add SCA as an option), and it never sees your runtime config. Pair it with SCA, secrets scanning and DAST.
  6. Running H2 in production. It's for demos only. Use PostgreSQL.

Rolling it out to a real team

The rollout plan that works tends to look like this:

Four steps, and the gate only turns on in week 3, after people have had time to get curious.

  1. Week 1, observe. Turn on scanning in CI, but don't block anything. Let people look at the dashboard and get curious.
  2. Week 2, install the IDE plugin. Get every developer on SonarQube for IDE in connected mode, so their editor uses the same rules as the server. Catching issues while typing is far less annoying than catching them in CI.
  3. Week 3, enable the gate on new code only. Use "Sonar way" as-is. Announce it, explain Clean as You Code, and answer questions.
  4. Ongoing, review together. Spend fifteen minutes in a retro now and then looking at hotspots and false positives. Tune the profile as a team.

The pattern underneath: make the tool a teammate, not a cop. Developers adopt tools that make them better at their job. They route around tools that only make them slower.

Wrapping up

Remember that search box from the start? With SonarQube in the pipeline, that PR would have come back red in a few minutes, with the exact line and a fix example attached. No incident, no Friday night, no awkward meeting.

That's the whole promise of SAST: catch the boring, predictable, expensive mistakes while they're still cheap. Not because developers are careless, but because humans are bad at spotting the same pattern for the thousandth time, and machines are great at it.

title: Check a CSV's missing-data contract before drawing a line
summary:
A parser can read every row successfully and still pass the wrong meaning to a plotting step. Consider six time records with response values 2, 3, NA, 0, 4, 5. The third value is missing. The fourth is an observed zero. Replacing one with the other changes the scientific meaning; deleting the missing record can also change the continuity of a line plot.

This is a self-written synthetic teaching example, not a dataset from a study, a customer result, or the output of an installed research Skill. We are the RigorMed team. The calculation below was actually run locally with Python's standard library; it does not use a model, paid service, or production research task.

Freeze what the file means

For this file only, the schema is time_h,response_au. Time is in hours; response is in arbitrary units. The exact token NA means missing. Numeric zero means observed zero. Rows are in strictly increasing time order. They describe one sequence, so the number of rows is not automatically an independent sample size.

Those rules are declared inputs, not guesses learned by the parser. If a source uses -999, an empty field, or another code, confirm its meaning and change the contract explicitly. Do not extend this example into a universal CSV cleaner.

Inspect without rewriting the source

The code retains each original token alongside a parsed value. Missing values become None in the inspection structure; the source CSV remains unchanged. It also rejects non-finite numbers and time reversals under this particular declared schema.

import csv
import io
import math

raw = """time_h,response_au
0,2
1,3
2,NA
3,0
4,4
5,5
"""
reader = csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(raw))
assert reader.fieldnames == ["time_h", "response_au"]
source_rows = list(reader)
checked = []
previous_time = None
for row in source_rows:
    t = float(row["time_h"])
    assert math.isfinite(t)
    assert previous_time is None or t > previous_time
    previous_time = t
    token = row["response_au"]
    value = None if token == "NA" else float(token)
    assert value is None or math.isfinite(value)
    checked.append((t, token, value))

missing_times = [t for t, token, value in checked if value is None]
observed = [value for t, token, value in checked if value is not None]
zero_times = [t for t, token, value in checked if value == 0]
