title: How I Clone My Own Voice on a Laptop With No GPU (Qwen3-TTS)
summary:
Key takeaways

  • A laptop with no GPU can run Qwen3-TTS voice cloning. Expect 3 to 6 seconds of computing per second of speech.
  • Use reference clips of 7 to 15 seconds. About 30 seconds in total was enough for me.
  • If your reference is casual talking, use x-vector only mode, or the clone will copy your hesitations.
  • Generate 3 to 5 takes per line and pick by where the pauses fall.

Tested on: Windows 11 laptop, Intel Core i9-13900H, 32 GB RAM, integrated graphics only (no NVIDIA GPU). Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base, qwen-tts 0.1.1, Python 3.11.

I post short animated videos that explain AI topics, narrated in Chinese. Recording the narration was the slowest part of every video. I stumble, re-record, and takes from different days don't sound the same. I wanted to type the script and get narration in my own voice.

Claude Code, an AI coding assistant, set this up on my laptop. I described what I wanted, listened to the results and made the calls. You can skip the code blocks; the settings that mattered are explained in plain words.

What I used

The model is Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base, an open-source text-to-speech model from Alibaba's Qwen team (Apache-2.0 license, code at github.com/Qwen/Qwen3-TTS). The "Base" version is the one that clones voices. I downloaded the weights from ModelScope, which was by far the fastest source where I live.

It runs through the qwen-tts Python package, version 0.1.1, in a Python 3.11 virtual environment. My system Python was newer than the machine-learning packages supported, so a separate 3.11 environment saved a lot of trouble.

Everything runs on the CPU in float32, with no CUDA and no NVIDIA card.

Step 1: Reference audio from a recording I already had

I didn't record anything new. I had a long screen recording where I was talking, and I cut three clips from it, about 33 seconds in total.

Longer clips sounded more like me. Clips of 7 to 15 seconds gave a clearly closer match than 4-second clips.

If there is music or noise behind your voice, remove it first. On my CPU, the BS-Roformer separation model needed about two hours for three minutes of audio. The Kim_Vocal_2 model in the audio-separator package did the same job in about three minutes.

Step 2: The setting that decides whether it sounds fluent

Qwen3-TTS Base can clone a voice in two ways:

Mode What you give it What it copies
ICL (the default) One clip plus its exact transcript Your voice and the way you spoke in that clip
x-vector only One or more clips, no transcript Only the sound of your voice

I started with ICL because it's the default. The problem was my reference clip: unscripted talking, with hesitations and uneven pace. The clone copied that too. Every line came out with the same stop-start rhythm, and it didn't sound fluent.

Switching to x-vector only mode fixed it. The model keeps my voice but uses its own steadier pacing, which is what narration needs. Since no transcript is needed, I could also feed it several clips at once.

If your reference is clean read-aloud speech, ICL may be fine. If it's casual talking, try x-vector first.

This is a simplified version of the script on my laptop:

import numpy as np, soundfile as sf, torch
from qwen_tts import Qwen3TTSModel

torch.set_num_threads(14)  # how many CPU threads to use

model = Qwen3TTSModel.from_pretrained(
    "models/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base", device_map="cpu", dtype=torch.float32
)

# Join a few clips of my voice (mono WAV) with a short silence between them
voice, sr = sf.read("my_voice.wav", dtype="float32")
gap = np.zeros(int(0.25 * sr), np.float32)
clips = [(12.0, 23.5), (61.0, 72.7), (130.2, 141.1)]  # start, end in seconds
parts = []
for start, end in clips:
    parts += [voice[int(start * sr):int(end * sr)], gap]
ref = np.concatenate(parts)

# x-vector only: copy the voice, not the rhythm. No transcript needed.
prompt = model.create_voice_clone_prompt(
    ref_audio=(ref, sr), ref_text=None, x_vector_only_mode=True
)

wavs, out_sr = model.generate_voice_clone(
    text=["大家好，今天聊聊怎么用 AI 给视频配音。"],
    language=["Chinese"],
    voice_clone_prompt=prompt,
)
sf.write("line01.wav", wavs[0], out_sr)

For ICL mode you pass one clip, its exact transcript as ref_text, and x_vector_only_mode=False.

Step 3: Make several takes and keep the best one

The same line comes out a little different every time. Some takes pause in the right places, some rush through a comma. So I generate every line 3 to 5 times and pick one.

What I listen for: does it pause at the commas, and does it avoid long gaps in the middle of a phrase. That matters more than small differences in tone.

With twenty-odd lines and several takes each, listening to everything gets tiring. So a script ranks the takes first:

  • It transcribes each take with a speech recognizer (Paraformer, for Chinese) and compares it with the script, to catch swallowed or wrong words.
  • It measures how close the voice is to a separate sample of my real voice that wasn't used for cloning (CAM++ speaker verification).
  • It counts the pauses and compares them with the commas in the line.

Then I only listen to the top few.

How fast is it on a CPU?

From my logs, generating up to six lines per batch: roughly 3 to 6 seconds of computing for each second of speech. One batch produced 37 seconds of speech in 127 seconds; another produced 24 seconds in 147 seconds.

For a two-minute narration that means about 7 to 12 minutes per take, or roughly half an hour for three takes. It's slow, but it runs in the background. Loading the model also takes time, so I generate all the lines in one run.

Smaller things that helped

Some Chinese characters have more than one pronunciation, and the model sometimes picks the wrong one. When that happens I swap in a same-sounding character in the text sent to the model and keep the correct word in the subtitles. For example, 长连接 became 常连接, and 回调 became 回掉.

Not every video needs my voice, either. For quick news videos I use a preset voice from the CustomVoice version of the same model, which needs no reference audio.

Only clone voices you have permission to use

Clone your own voice, or a voice whose owner has agreed. Don't publish a cloned voice of anyone else.

Would a paid service be easier?

Probably. Hosted services such as ElevenLabs need no setup. I have since run the same script through ElevenLabs' free plan, and its stock Mandarin voices sounded more natural than my clone: ElevenLabs free plan vs a local open-source model.

title: 2,000 TripAdvisor reviews in 62 seconds for one cent: what one Times Square hotel's guests actually complain about
summary:
TripAdvisor shows a hotel's all-time score at the top of the page. For an old hotel with 18,000 reviews, that number mostly describes stays from years ago. If you want to know what guests say now, you need the recent reviews themselves, in a table.

So we pulled them. One run of our TripAdvisor Reviews Scraper on Apify, pointed at the Hotel Edison Times Square, asking for 2,000 reviews:

  • Time: 62 seconds.
  • Cost: $0.0096 of compute on our side. A user pays $0.50 per 1,000 reviews on the Starter tier, so this run is $1.00 for anyone else.
  • Coverage: 2,000 reviews from 12 Dec 2024 to 3 Nov 2026, plus one row for the hotel itself.

Every number below comes from that one run. Reviews are written by members of the public, so this post shows counts only: no reviewer names and no quotes from reviews.

The input 

{
  "startUrls": [
    { "url": "https://www.tripadvisor.com/Hotel_Review-g60763-d93437-Reviews-Hotel_Edison_Times_Square-New_York_City_New_York.html" }
  ],
  "maxReviewsPerPlace": 2000
}

Any TripAdvisor review page works the same way: hotels, restaurants and attractions, on any TripAdvisor country site. Filters are optional: ratings (for example only 1 and 2 stars), reviewsSince, languages, tripTypes (family, couples, solo, business, friends), reviewsContaining and sortBy.

From Python:

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("locaihost/tripadvisor-reviews").call(run_input={
    "startUrls": [{"url": "https://www.tripadvisor.com/Hotel_Review-g60763-d93437-Reviews-Hotel_Edison_Times_Square-New_York_City_New_York.html"}],
    "maxReviewsPerPlace": 2000,
})
rows = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())
reviews = [r for r in rows if r["type"] == "review"]

Each review row has the rating, title, full text, language (and whether TripAdvisor machine-translated it), published date, travel month, trip type, sub-ratings when given, helpful votes, photo count and the hotel's reply. Reviewer names are off by default. The place row carries the address, coordinates, all-time rating and histogram, sub-scores, the "#169 of 529 hotels" ranking, amenities, and three numbers computed from the reviews you collected: owner reply rate, average reply lag and the rating over the last 90 days.

Finding 1: the all-time score hides two good years

Reviews Average 5 stars
All time (TripAdvisor's own histogram) 18,836 3.9 40%
Latest 2,000 (Dec 2024 to Nov 2026) 2,000 4.43 71%

The headline 3.9 is dragged down by older stays: 2,482 of the hotel's one and two-star reviews are in the all-time histogram, and only 176 of them are in the last two years. Month by month, the recent average sits between 4.18 (September 2026) and 4.67 (April 2025), with no trend down.

If you compare hotels by their all-time score, an older property that has improved looks worse than it is. A 90-day or 12-month average from the raw reviews is fairer, and it's one column in the output (ratingLast90d: 4.35 over 250 reviews here).

Finding 2: who is happiest

Trip type Reviews Average
Solo 93 4.78
Friends 256 4.68
Family 620 4.58
Couples 262 4.47
Business 124 4.34
Not given 645 4.14

Business travellers rate it lowest of the groups that say why they came. Reviewers who don't pick a trip type are the least happy of all, which is common: an angry reviewer fills in fewer optional fields.

Finding 3: what the bad reviews are about

We split the reviews into 176 low (1 or 2 stars) and 1,701 high (4 or 5 stars) and counted how many in each group mention a word at least once (whole words only):

Mentioned Low reviews High reviews
noise / noisy 23% 7%
bathroom 26% 8%
old / dated / outdated 20% 5%
check-in 17% 8%
window 16% 1%
price / expensive / overpriced 18% 6%
rude 12% 0%
fee / fees 11% 1%
air conditioning / AC 11% 2%
dirty 9% 0%
staff 44% 54%
location 34% 54%
clean 15% 33%

The pattern is clear even with simple word counts. Happy guests talk about the staff and the location. Unhappy guests talk about the room itself (bathroom, noise through the windows, an old building, the air conditioning) and about the front desk (check-in, rude, fees). "Staff" shows up in both groups, because staff are the reason for both the best and the worst reviews.

This is the cheapest version of the analysis. With the full text in a dataframe, the next step is an embedding or topic model over the 176 low reviews, which takes a few seconds on a laptop.

Finding 4: the hotel answers almost everything

1,991 of the 2,000 reviews have a reply from the hotel (99.6%), including 175 of the 176 low ones, and the average reply comes 4.6 days after the review. That's a well-run reply process. For a competitor analysis, reply rate and reply lag are two of the most telling columns: they show which hotels have someone watching their reviews.

What it doesn't do

  • It reads what a logged-out visitor can see. A list stops at about 10,000 reviews; for bigger places, run it per star rating to go deeper.
  • Machine-translated reviews are marked (machineTranslated). 161 of these 2,000 were translations; filter them out with languages if you only want originals.
  • It doesn't name staff. Names in the hotel's replies are replaced with [name removed].

Try it

The Actor is locaihost/tripadvisor-reviews on the Apify Store: $0.50 per 1,000 reviews and $1 per 1,000 places on the Starter tier, cheaper on the higher tiers, and links that aren't a TripAdvisor place are never charged. If you run it and something looks wrong, open an issue on the Actor page and we'll fix it the same day.

title: I Wrote a Python Script That Cleans Up Any Messy Folder — and It Never Deletes Anything by Default
summary:
Everyone has that one folder. Downloads, Desktop, some project directory — hundreds of files, no structure, and the thought of sorting it by hand is so dull you just... don't.

I wrote a small Python script that does it for you. It sorts a folder's files into subfolders by type, and the important part is in the title: by default, it changes nothing. It only shows you what it would do. You have to explicitly tell it to move files.

What it does

Point it at a folder and it sorts every file into one of six categories:

Folder Extensions
Images .jpg, .jpeg, .png, .gif, .webp, .svg
Documents .pdf, .doc, .docx, .txt, .md
Spreadsheets .csv, .xls, .xlsx, .ods
Archives .zip, .tar, .gz, .rar, .7z
Code .py, .js, .html, .css, .json
Others anything else

No dependencies beyond the standard library — just argparse, shutil, and pathlib. No install step at all.

Usage 

python file_organizer.py ~/Downloads            # dry run, no changes
python file_organizer.py ~/Downloads --apply    # actually move files

The dry run prints lines like would move: report.pdf -> Documents/ and finishes with a count. Only --apply performs the moves.

How it works

The whole script is built around one mapping and one function:

CATEGORIES = {
    "Images": {".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png", ".gif", ".webp", ".svg"},
    "Documents": {".pdf", ".doc", ".docx", ".txt", ".md"},
    "Spreadsheets": {".csv", ".xls", ".xlsx", ".ods"},
    "Archives": {".zip", ".tar", ".gz", ".rar", ".7z"},
    "Code": {".py", ".js", ".html", ".css", ".json"},
}

def category_for(path):
    """Return the category folder name for a file's extension."""
    for name, extensions in CATEGORIES.items():
        if path.suffix.lower() in extensions:
            return name
    return "Others"

Extensions are lowercased before matching, so Photo.JPG and photo.jpg land in the same folder. Anything unknown falls into Others rather than being skipped silently — a file you can't find is worse than a file in a misc folder.

The organising function keeps the dry-run and apply paths in one place, so they can never drift apart:

def organize(folder, apply=False):
    folder = Path(folder)
    if not folder.is_dir():
        print(f"error: {folder} is not a folder", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1
    moved = 0
    for path in sorted(folder.iterdir()):
        if not path.is_file():
            continue  # never touch subfolders
        target_dir = folder / category_for(path)
        target = target_dir / path.name
        if apply:
            target_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
            shutil.move(str(path), str(target))
            print(f"moved: {path.name} -> {target_dir.name}/")
        else:
            print(f"would move: {path.name} -> {target_dir.name}/")
        moved += 1
    mode = "moved" if apply else "would move (dry run — use --apply to move)"
    print(f"{moved} file(s) {mode}")
    return 0

Three safety decisions are doing the quiet work here:

  1. Dry run is the default. The destructive action requires an explicit flag. If you run it by accident, nothing happens — you just get a preview.
  2. It never touches subfolders. Only files directly in the folder are moved. Your existing structure stays intact.
  3. It never deletes. Files are moved, not removed. If a category looks wrong, everything is still there, one folder away.

Three lessons I'd pass on

  1. Make the safe behaviour the default. A script that moves files should have to be talked into it. Dry-run-first is a design decision, not a feature — and it's the reason I'd trust this on a real Downloads folder.
  2. Small scripts beat small apps. This is about 70 lines and has no dependencies. It doesn't need a GUI, a config file, or a scheduler to be useful.
  3. Print what you're doing. Every move gets a line of output, and the run ends with a count. When a script touches your files, silence is a bug.

This is the second tool in my Python Automation Toolkit — the first scrapes a catalogue into a clean Excel report, and this one tidies the folder that report lands in. Next, I'll write about the project that taught me the most: a RAG-powered assistant that answers questions about Pakistani electricity bills.

title: How to Solve the Cloudflare 5-Second Challenge in Python for Automated Testing
summary:
You already have Cloudflare Turnstile handled. But then you hit a different wall: instead of a widget inside the page, the entire page is replaced by a full-screen "Verifying you are human" interstitial that never resolves for your script. That is the Cloudflare challenge page (the "5-second challenge" in a browser), and it needs a completely different API call than Turnstile does.

This walkthrough shows how to solve it with Kaptra's captcha API using the AntiCloudflareTask type: what parameters it needs, what comes back, and how to replay the result so your requests actually get through.

Widget vs full-page: know which one you are facing

These two Cloudflare defenses get confused all the time, and the fix for one does not work on the other:

  • Turnstile: an embedded widget in a form. You collect a sitekey from the page, send it with the URL, and receive a token to submit with the form.
  • The challenge page: the page itself is swapped for an interstitial. There is no sitekey anywhere. The solver has to pass the interstitial and return the resulting cookies, and those cookies are bound to the IP that earned them. That binding is exactly why this task type requires you to pass your own proxy.

Quick diagnostic: if your response body is mostly a "Just a moment..." page, it is the second case. Read on.

What the solved task hands you

When polling completes, solution contains cookies: the clearance material for that protected page. The flow from there:

  1. Create an AntiCloudflareTask with the protected URL and your HTTP proxy.
  2. Poll getTaskResult until status is ready.
  3. Attach solution["cookies"] to your session and send your real requests through the same proxy from step 1. The clearance was issued for that IP, so keep using it.

Full Python example 

import time
import requests
# ---
BASE_URL = "https://api.kaptra.ai"
API_KEY = "YOUR_KAPTRA_API_KEY"
# ---
def solve_cloudflare_challenge(website_url: str, proxy: str) -> dict:
    # 1. create the task; proxy is required for this type (HTTP only)
    resp = requests.post(
        f"{BASE_URL}/createTask",
        json={
            "clientKey": API_KEY,
            "task": {
                "type": "AntiCloudflareTask",
                "websiteURL": website_url,
                "proxy": proxy,
            },
        },
    ).json()
    if resp.get("errorId"):
        raise RuntimeError(f"createTask failed: {resp.get('errorCode')}")
    task_id = resp["taskId"]
    # 2. poll every 1-2s, max 120 queries per task
    for _ in range(120):
        result = requests.post(
            f"{BASE_URL}/getTaskResult",
            json={"clientKey": API_KEY, "taskId": task_id},
        ).json()
        status = result.get("status")
        if status == "ready":
            return result["solution"]  # {"cookies": ...}
        if status == "failure":
            raise RuntimeError(f"task failed: {result.get('errorCode')}")
        # processing (or CAPTCHA_NOT_READY): keep polling
        time.sleep(1.5)
    raise TimeoutError("gave up after 120 polls")
# ---
if __name__ == "__main__":
    my_proxy = "http://USER:PASS@HOST:PORT"
    solution = solve_cloudflare_challenge(
        "https://www.example.com/protected", my_proxy
    )
    print(solution["cookies"])
    # 3. attach these cookies to your session and keep
    #    sending requests through that same proxy

Same client skeleton as the Turnstile flow: createTask, then poll every 1 to 2 seconds with a ceiling of 120 queries. CAPTCHA_NOT_READY means the worker is still on it; status settles at ready or failure.

Gotchas worth knowing before you ship

HTTP proxies only. The docs state it plainly: a public HTTP proxy is required and SOCKS is rejected. If your stack is SOCKS-only, front it with HTTP or use a different provider for these tasks.

Failure handling. Average solve time is under 10 seconds, so 120 polls at 1.5 second intervals is a wide margin. A failure surfaces as ERROR_CAPTCHA_UNSOLVABLE; retrying once with the same parameters is the normal move, because billing is per solved task.

Cost. $1.20 per 1,000 successful solves, nothing for failures or timeouts, no monthly fee, no expiring balance. New Kaptra accounts start with $10 in test credit, enough to validate the whole flow before you commit.

HTTP codes carry no signal. Every response is HTTP 200. The verdict lives in errorId (0 or 1) and errorCode in the JSON. If your code already speaks that envelope, nothing to change.

Summary

Widget: sitekey in, token out, submit with the form. Challenge page: your HTTP proxy in, cookies out, replay through that proxy. Different inputs, different outputs, same create-then-poll loop underneath.

  • Site: kaptra.ai
  • AntiCloudflareTask docs: kaptra.ai/docs

title: Chat memory as a 41.9 MB file: building on MemT-1.0-Nano's save and reload
summary:
Most chat backends resend the whole transcript to the model on every turn. MemT-1.0-Nano, an open model from MemTensor whose base model is the Qwen team's Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, works on a different contract. Turns you flag are folded into a block of numbers that never grows, and that block can be written to disk. In the test, a saved memory was loaded into a new session holding zero messages, and the model got all nine recall questions right. Every saved file weighed 41,944,024 bytes.

The tables and setup are in the full MemT-1.0-Nano memory file write-up on inferencekey.com; here is what you would build around it.

Your code chooses what the model keeps

The session API in MemTensor's modeling_memt.py treats remembering as an explicit call. Pass enable_memory=True and that turn is committed into the memory state and its text discarded. Other turns stay in the session as ordinary text. Shortened from the model card:

session.chat("", enable_memory=True, enable_thinking=False)
session.save_state("dana.safetensors")
restored = model.create_session(tokenizer, state="dana.safetensors")
print(len(restored.messages))  # 0

Which turns deserve the flag is product logic you write. Tokens are the word pieces a model reads, and in the restored session the input for each question went from 27 tokens to 210 over four questions, because the questions themselves were never flagged and piled up as text. Flag nothing and the transcript is back.

By default save_state will not overwrite an existing file, so plan your naming.

Disk gets worse, rereading gets better

As text on disk, the made-up bakery owner's history in the test was 107 tokens, a few hundred bytes. The memory file is 41.9 MB no matter what.

It competes instead with the working memory a regular model rebuilds from the whole history and holds on the GPU while the session is open. According to the storage arithmetic in the MemT-1.0-Nano research post, the fixed file only beats it once the history passes roughly 2,000 tokens, and at 128K tokens it is about 64 times smaller. For speed, MemTensor's paper has Nano losing on short histories, breaking even near 32,000 tokens and pulling ahead by about 1.86 times at 128K. The test measured neither.

On one A100 80 GB, loading took 1.35 to 1.99 seconds and saving 0.66 to 1.02. Generating was slow: answering a "remember" turn with 128 tokens took about 13 seconds on the stock Hugging Face code, without the optional faster GPU components and with no tuning.

Two traps worth knowing first

Compressing to 8 bits does not get you onto a smaller GPU. The weights normally run in bf16, a 16-bit number format. With the A100 limited to what a 48 GB card offers, the 8-bit load ran out of memory after asking for about 64 GiB. With the limit removed it loaded, and the first "remember" call then died with a dtype (number type) mismatch. The cause is in the architecture. Each layer holds 256 experts (sub-networks the model picks between per token), stored as fused 3D parameters rather than nn.Linear layers, so the bitsandbytes 8-bit library skips them and the saving is about 2 GiB. The 48 GB case was emulated with a cap, and no other shrinking method was tried. With no official compressed release, budget for an 80 GB GPU.

Load by repo id, not from the Hugging Face cache folder. trust_remote_code lets Transformers, the Hugging Face Python library, run the model's own Python files. Pointing it at the downloaded snapshot directory fails with "file not found": Transformers follows the modeling_memt.py symlink into blobs/ and looks for the relative import there. Loading by repo id with a pinned revision avoids it.

Behind an API, the state file will not fit a result payload capped at 8 MB. In the InferenceKey backend it stays on the worker's disk (the worker is the program running the model on the GPU machine), and the API returns its size and sha256.

Two licenses, two answers

The Nano weights carry Apache-2.0, which permits commercial use. MemTensor's own code on GitHub, the two-GPU memt-sglang server included, is under PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0. The test ran the Apache-2.0 code from the Hugging Face repo, the slow path.

What a pilot should measure

Every recall question in the test asked for a short fact given to the model moments earlier. That shows the round trip works, not memory over months. MemTensor is open about this: text-based memory systems still lead, above all on long histories where a precise detail has to be found. On the LongMemEval-S benchmark the paper puts Nano at 32.6, while sending the whole conversation scores 76.8. On your own data, check:

  • Exact details from early in long histories, compared with a text store.
  • Whether many memory writes over time push older facts out. Nobody has tested it.
  • Behavior with several sessions at once. The test sent one request at a time.

The hosted InferenceKey endpoint was not tested either: the run used a local test copy of InferenceKey and a worker on a GPU on our cloud.

Credit goes to MemTensor for the model, the trained memory block, the session API and the MemT-1.0 paper, to the Qwen team for the base model, and to Hugging Face Transformers for running the custom code. We found the model through the AI Search news video and an r/LocalLLaMA thread. We wrote the custom backend, found the load fix and ran the tests. To repeat the round trip on your own NVIDIA machine, the SDK example for the MemT-1.0-Nano backend runs it end to end.

The GPU memory results, every timing, the paper's benchmark numbers and the open issues are in the MemT-1.0-Nano research article on inferencekey.com.

The tables and setup are in the full MemT-1.0-Nano memory file write-up on inferencekey.com; here is what you would build around it.

Your code chooses what the model keeps

The session API in MemTensor's modeling_memt.py treats remembering as an explicit call. Pass enable_memory=True and that turn is committed into the memory state and its text discarded. Other turns stay in the session as ordinary text. Shortened from the model card:

session.chat("", enable_memory=True, enable_thinking=False)
session.save_state("dana.safetensors")
restored = model.create_session(tokenizer, state="dana.safetensors")
print(len(restored.messages))  # 0

Which turns deserve the flag is product logic you write. Tokens are the word pieces a model reads, and in the restored session the input for each question went from 27 tokens to 210 over four questions, because the questions themselves were never flagged and piled up as text. Flag nothing and the transcript is back.

By default save_state will not overwrite an existing file, so plan your naming.

Disk gets worse, rereading gets better

As text on disk, the made-up bakery owner's history in the test was 107 tokens, a few hundred bytes. The memory file is 41.9 MB no matter what.

It competes instead with the working memory a regular model rebuilds from the whole history and holds on the GPU while the session is open. According to the storage arithmetic in the MemT-1.0-Nano research post, the fixed file only beats it once the history passes roughly 2,000 tokens, and at 128K tokens it is about 64 times smaller. For speed, MemTensor's paper has Nano losing on short histories, breaking even near 32,000 tokens and pulling ahead by about 1.86 times at 128K. The test measured neither.

On one A100 80 GB, loading took 1.35 to 1.99 seconds and saving 0.66 to 1.02. Generating was slow: answering a "remember" turn with 128 tokens took about 13 seconds on the stock Hugging Face code, without the optional faster GPU components and with no tuning.

Two traps worth knowing first

Compressing to 8 bits does not get you onto a smaller GPU. The weights normally run in bf16, a 16-bit number format. With the A100 limited to what a 48 GB card offers, the 8-bit load ran out of memory after asking for about 64 GiB. With the limit removed it loaded, and the first "remember" call then died with a dtype (number type) mismatch. The cause is in the architecture. Each layer holds 256 experts (sub-networks the model picks between per token), stored as fused 3D parameters rather than nn.Linear layers, so the bitsandbytes 8-bit library skips them and the saving is about 2 GiB. The 48 GB case was emulated with a cap, and no other shrinking method was tried. With no official compressed release, budget for an 80 GB GPU.

Load by repo id, not from the Hugging Face cache folder. trust_remote_code lets Transformers, the Hugging Face Python library, run the model's own Python files. Pointing it at the downloaded snapshot directory fails with "file not found": Transformers follows the modeling_memt.py symlink into blobs/ and looks for the relative import there. Loading by repo id with a pinned revision avoids it.

Behind an API, the state file will not fit a result payload capped at 8 MB. In the InferenceKey backend it stays on the worker's disk (the worker is the program running the model on the GPU machine), and the API returns its size and sha256.

Two licenses, two answers

The Nano weights carry Apache-2.0, which permits commercial use. MemTensor's own code on GitHub, the two-GPU memt-sglang server included, is under PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0. The test ran the Apache-2.0 code from the Hugging Face repo, the slow path.

What a pilot should measure

Every recall question in the test asked for a short fact given to the model moments earlier. That shows the round trip works, not memory over months. MemTensor is open about this: text-based memory systems still lead, above all on long histories where a precise detail has to be found. On the LongMemEval-S benchmark the paper puts Nano at 32.6, while sending the whole conversation scores 76.8. On your own data, check:

  • Exact details from early in long histories, compared with a text store.
  • Whether many memory writes over time push older facts out. Nobody has tested it.
  • Behavior with several sessions at once. The test sent one request at a time.

The hosted InferenceKey endpoint was not tested either: the run used a local test copy of InferenceKey and a worker on a GPU on our cloud.

Credit goes to MemTensor for the model, the trained memory block, the session API and the MemT-1.0 paper, to the Qwen team for the base model, and to Hugging Face Transformers for running the custom code. We found the model through the AI Search news video and an r/LocalLLaMA thread. We wrote the custom backend, found the load fix and ran the tests. To repeat the round trip on your own NVIDIA machine, the SDK example for the MemT-1.0-Nano backend runs it end to end.

The GPU memory results, every timing, the paper's benchmark numbers and the open issues are in the MemT-1.0-Nano research article on inferencekey.com.

title: I Built a Scraper That Turns 1,000 Book Listings Into a Clean Excel Report — Here's How
summary:
Most "learn web scraping" tutorials stop at printing a few titles to the terminal. That never felt like a finished tool to me, so I built one that goes all the way: scrape a catalogue, clean the data, and hand over a formatted Excel report someone could actually use.

The stack is plain Python: requests, BeautifulSoup, pandas, and openpyxl. No frameworks, no paid APIs. The target is books.toscrape.com, a site built specifically for practising scraping — so everything here is on a public practice page, not a real store.

What you end up with

Running two scripts produces:

  • data/books_raw.csv — the raw scrape, one row per book
  • data/books_clean.csv — the same data, cleaned
  • data/books_clean.xlsx — a formatted Excel report: bold headers, filters, a frozen top row, and sensible column widths

The full run collects 1,000 books, and the cleaned report's average price comes out at £35.07.

Step 0: Setup 

pip install requests beautifulsoup4 pandas openpyxl

Three files: scraper.py (collect), clean_export.py (clean + export), and a data/ folder for the outputs.

Step 1: Scrape every page, not just the first one

A catalogue scraper that only reads page 1 is a demo, not a tool. The real job is walking the pagination until there is no "next" link left. The core loop does exactly that:

def scrape(max_pages=None):
    all_books = []
    page = 1
    while True:
        url = CATALOGUE_URL.format(page)
        response = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, timeout=20)
        response.raise_for_status()
        response.encoding = "utf-8"
        books, has_next = parse_page(response.text, url)
        all_books.extend(books)
        if not has_next:
            break
        page += 1
        if max_pages and page > max_pages:
            break
        time.sleep(0.2)  # be polite to the server
    return all_books

Each page is parsed with one function that pulls five fields out of every book card:

def parse_page(html, page_url):
    soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser")
    books = []
    for article in soup.select("article.product_pod"):
        title = article.h3.a["title"].strip()
        price_text = article.select_one("p.price_color").get_text(strip=True)
        rating_word = article.select_one("p.star-rating")["class"][1]
        availability = article.select_one("p.instock").get_text(strip=True)
        rel_url = article.h3.a["href"]
        books.append({
            "title": title,
            "price": price_text,
            "rating": rating_word,
            "availability": availability,
            "url": urljoin(page_url, rel_url),
        })
    has_next = soup.select_one("li.next a") is not None
    return books, has_next

Three details worth calling out, because each one bit me or would have:

  1. The £ encoding gotcha. This site doesn't declare its charset, so requests guesses Latin-1 and corrupts the £ sign. The pages are actually UTF-8, so one line — response.encoding = "utf-8" — fixes it before parsing. If your scraped prices ever look like Â£51.77, this is almost certainly why.
  2. Be polite. A 0.2 second sleep between pages and an honest User-Agent (python-automation-toolkit/1.0 (learning project)) cost nothing and keep you from hammering someone else's server. Scraping fast is not a skill; scraping without getting blocked is.
  3. Relative URLs. Book links on the page are relative, so urljoin(page_url, rel_url) turns them into full URLs you can actually click later.

Run it with python scraper.py (or --pages 5 for a quick test run), and you get data/books_raw.csv with 1,000 rows.

Step 2: Clean the data before anyone sees it

Raw scraped data is never report-ready. Prices are strings with currency symbols (£51.77), ratings are words (Three), and availability is a sentence fragment. The cleaning step turns all of that into typed, analysable data:

RATING_MAP = {"One": 1, "Two": 2, "Three": 3, "Four": 4, "Five": 5}

def clean(df):
    df = df.copy()
    # "£51.77" -> 51.77 (drop anything that is not a digit or a dot)
    df["price"] = df["price"].astype(str).str.replace(r"[^0-9.]", "", regex=True)
    df["price"] = pd.to_numeric(df["price"], errors="coerce")
    df = df.dropna(subset=["price"])
    # "Three" -> 3
    df["rating"] = df["rating"].map(RATING_MAP)
    # "In stock" -> True, anything else -> False
    df["in_stock"] = df["availability"].str.contains("In stock", na=False)
    df = df.drop(columns=["availability"])
    df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=["title", "url"])
    return df

The pattern here is worth stealing for any scrape: strip, convert with errors="coerce" (bad values become NaN instead of crashing the run), drop the rows that didn't convert, and drop duplicates on a sensible key — here, title + URL.

Step 3: Export an Excel file a human would enjoy opening

A CSV is fine for machines. If a person is going to read the report, formatting matters — and it's only a few lines with openpyxl:

def write_excel(df, path):
    with pd.ExcelWriter(path, engine="openpyxl") as writer:
        df.to_excel(writer, sheet_name="Books", index=False)
        sheet = writer.sheets["Books"]
        for cell in sheet[1]:
            cell.font = Font(bold=True)
        sheet.auto_filter.ref = sheet.dimensions
        sheet.freeze_panes = "A2"
        widths = {"title": 55, "price": 10, "rating": 10,
                  "in_stock": 10, "url": 60}
        for idx, col in enumerate(df.columns, start=1):
            sheet.column_dimensions[get_column_letter(idx)].width = (
                widths.get(col, 20)
            )

Bold headers, filters, a frozen top row, columns wide enough for the content. That's the difference between "here's a file" and "here's a report."

python clean_export.py also prints a short summary: book count, average price, how many are in stock, and the rating mix.

The result

Output Contents
books_raw.csv 1,000 books, raw strings
books_clean.csv 1,000 books, typed and deduplicated
books_clean.xlsx Same data, formatted and filterable

Average price across the catalogue: £35.07.

Three lessons I'd pass on

  1. Scrape practice sites to learn. Real sites have terms of service, rate limits, and anti-bot measures. Learn the mechanics on a site built for it, and only scrape public pages with permission when real data is involved.
  2. The pipeline is the project. Scraping is the easy third. Cleaning and presenting the data is where a script becomes a tool someone would pay for.
  3. Small, polite, honest scripts beat clever ones. A 0.2 second delay and a real User-Agent never got anyone blocked; pretending to be a browser did.

The full code is in my Python Automation Toolkit project, and the same scrape → clean → report pattern works for any tabular listing: products, jobs, or prices. Next, I'll write about the other half of the toolkit — a file organiser that tidies a messy downloads folder without ever deleting anything by default.

title: RagLeap Physical: A Simulation-First Safety Bridge for AI Agents
summary:
What should happen when an AI agent proposes an action that affects a physical-system simulation?

At RagLeap, we're exploring a controlled workflow:

AI proposes → Human approves → Safety limits are checked → Simulator verifies

RagLeap Physical is an open-source, pre-alpha Python project built around this idea.

🔗 GitHub: https://github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core/tree/main/packages/ragleap-physical

What it does

RagLeap Physical provides a simulation-first bridge between AI agents and physical-system simulators.

The project includes:

  • Safety envelopes
  • Exact-proposal approval
  • Dry runs
  • Runtime monitoring
  • Stop functionality
  • Audit logs
  • AI-facing tools
  • MCP server
  • Optional MuJoCo adapters
  • Workspace limits
  • Runnable simulation demos

The focus is not unrestricted AI control. It is controlled, observable interaction.

Release journey

v0.0.1 — Core bridge

The first release introduced the safety bridge, exact-proposal approval, runtime monitoring, audit logs, MCP tools, MuJoCo adapters, workspace limits, and simulation examples.

v0.0.2 — Operator console

The second release added a human operator console.

A named person can review pending proposals, approve the exact digest, apply the action, and stop.

The console is loopback-only, uses one token per person, and is not an AI tool.

v0.0.3 — Two-link workspace demo

The latest release adds:

examples/two_link_workspace_demo.py

The demo shows a two-link arm with one accepted workspace move and one refused move.

It also includes package metadata improvements and a fix for request handling in the operator console and MCP server.

Install 

pip install ragleap-physical==0.0.3

Optional extras:

pip install "ragleap-physical[mujoco]"
pip install "ragleap-physical[test]"
pip install "ragleap-physical[interop]"

Testing

The v0.0.3 release reports:

  • 255 tests passed with MuJoCo and the MCP SDK installed in Colab
  • GitHub CI on Python 3.10, 3.11, and 3.12

The Windows refusal-fix behavior is not yet verified.

Important limitations

This is pre-alpha and simulation-only.

It does not control real hardware. No real-robot or real-machine validation, safety certification, or regulatory compliance is claimed.

MuJoCo results are repeatable within one installed environment only. The wear-study and machine-tool numbers are invented.

Contribute

We welcome feedback and contributions from developers working on AI agents, simulation, robotics, MCP, and safety engineering.

Explore the package:

https://github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core/tree/main/packages/ragleap-physical

Install:

pip install ragleap-physical==0.0.3

AI proposes. Humans approve. The system verifies.
